By the present appeal, the appellant/ State seeks to assail the judgment and order dated 18 April 2006 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Thane, in Sessions Case No.68 of 2005, whereby the respondents/accused came to be acquitted of the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
2.

The prosecution case, in brief, is that the deceased, Nirmala, was married to Vikas Ghadge on 25 March 2003 and thereafter began residing with her husband and the present respondents at her matrimonial home.
At the time of the marriage, the parents of the deceased presented certain gold ornaments and household articles in accordance with prevailing social customs.

The prosecution alleges that the accused persons were dissatisfied with the articles so given and, on that account,
subjected the deceased to repeated taunts and mental harassment, contending that she had not brought additional articles such as a mixer, mattress and other household goods.
It is further alleged that the accused persistently pressurised the deceased to procure money and additional articles from her parental home.

. According to the prosecution, on 9 December 2004 the deceased telephoned her mother,
Indumati, requesting her to visit the matrimonial home.
When Indumati arrived, the deceased is stated to have informed her that her in-laws frequently taunted her by remarking that Vikas would have received a larger dowry had he married another woman.
The prosecution contends that such remarks caused the deceased considerable mental distress and anguish.
4. On the following day, the deceased sustained extensive burn injuries and was admitted to Shivaji Hospital for treatment.

It is alleged that she informed her mother that, following a quarrel with the The State Of Maharashtra vs Madhukar Nana Ghadge And Ors. on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167050953/
2 accused regarding money, she poured kerosene upon herself and set herself on fire.

sentences.text: The deceased had suffered approximately 87 per cent burn injuries and survived for about five days thereafter.
During this period, several statements came to be recorded.
A dying declaration was first recorded on 10 December 2004.
Thereafter, further statements were recorded on 14 December 2004 by a Special Executive Officer and by PSI Nikumbh after medical certification regarding her fitness to make such statements.
The latter statement was recorded after the mother of the deceased alleged that the earlier statement had been made under pressure from the accused.
Subsequently, on 15 December 2004, a formal complaint was lodged for the offence punishable under Section 498-A read with 34 of the IPC.

Upon the death of the deceased on 16 December 2004,
the offence punishable under Section 306 of the IPC came to be added.
6. Upon completion of investigation, a charge-sheet was filed against the accused.
The respondents denied the allegations and claimed to be tried.

In order to substantiate its case, the prosecution examined eleven witnesses, including Balkrishna, the father of the deceased (PW-1); Rangnath, the uncle of the deceased (PW-2); Indumati Garud, the mother of the deceased and the complainant (PW-3); Shraddha Shrikrishna Ghag, the Special Executive Officer who recorded one of the dying declarations (Exh. 28) (PW-4); Kausabai, the aunt of the deceased (PW-5); Chhaya, the paternal aunt of the deceased (PW-6); Swartha Garud, the grandfather of the deceased (PW- 7); Ganesh, the uncle of the deceased (PW-8); Pralhad Nikumbh, the police officer who recorded another dying declaration (Exh. 43) and conducted part of the investigation (PW-10); and Dr Chawala, the Medical Officer who examined the patient and certified her condition (PW-11).
7 . A f t e r t h e p r o s e c u t i o n e v i d e n c e c o n c l u d e d , t h e s t a t e m e n t s __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane.
3-apeal-868-2006.docx
of the accused were recorded under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, wherein the incriminating circumstances appearing against them were put to them.
The accused denied the same and, in their defence, examined Vikas, the husband of the deceased (DW-1).
Upon appreciation of the evidence on record, the learned trial Court acquitted the respondents of the charges.
Being aggrieved thereby, the State has preferred the present appeal.
8. This Court has given anxious consideration to the rival submissions advanced across the Bar and has carefully perused the entire record of the case.
9. At the outset, it is not in dispute that the death of Nirmala was suicidal in nature.
The defence has not challenged the genuineness of the documentary evidence on record, including the inquest panchanama, the post-mortem report and the spot panchanama.

The principal issue which,
however, arises for determination is whether the prosecution has succeeded in establishing a proximate and direct nexus between the alleged conduct of the accused and the suicidal death of the deceased.

sentences.text: 3 10. The testimony of PW-1 does not substantiate any specific or consistent allegation regarding unlawful demand of dowry or cruelty on that account.
His evidence merely refers to a __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx
solitary incident in which the deceased allegedly informed him that her mother-in-law had slapped her after a glass container was broken.
Significantly, this incident does not find mention in his earlier statement recorded by the police, thereby constituting a material omission which adversely affects the credibility of his testimony.
Apart from this vague and uncorroborated allegation, the evidence of PW-1 does not disclose any concrete instance of persistent harassment or coercion in connection with any alleged dowry demand.

On the contrary,
his cross-examination reveals that the families of the accused and the complainant were acquainted even prior to the marriage, a circumstance which diminishes the probability of the alleged dowry-related hostility.
11. It further emerges from the record that the deceased had been suffering from mental illness for a considerable period.

The testimony of PW-1 itself indicates that Nirmala had been undergoing treatment at Shivaji Hospital, Kalwa since the year 2002 and that such treatment continued even after her marriage, the accused themselves taking her to the hospital.
The discharge card of the said hospital (Exh.26), duly proved through the defence witness DW-1 and admitted by PW-3 in cross-examination, records the diagnosis as "psychotic disorder".
This documentary evidence clearly establishes that __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx
the deceased had been under psychiatric treatment for several years.

Although certain relatives attempted to deny the existence of any mental illness,
their evidence contains evasive answers and admissions which unmistakably indicate that the deceased was indeed undergoing treatment for a psychiatric condition.
The existence of such a disorder assumes considerable significance while examining the circumstances leading to the suicide.
12. The testimony of PW-2 also fails to materially advance the prosecution case.
He merely stated that the accused used to scold the deceased on trivial matters and that she would become nervous.
His evidence does not disclose any instance of dowry demand or sustained cruelty.
Moreover, he admitted that when he visited the house of the accused on the night preceding the incident, the deceased made no complaint of ill-treatment and went to sleep after taking medicines.
His testimony therefore does not support the allegation that the deceased was subjected to harassment immediately prior to the occurrence.
13. Similarly, the testimony of PW-3 is marked by inconsistencies and generalised allegations.

Although she asserted that the deceased had disclosed harassment relating to dowry, her account stands contradicted by the evidence of PW- __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx 2, who accompanied her during the visit on 9 December 2004 and categorically stated that the deceased did not disclose any such harassment.
This material contradiction strikes at the root of the prosecution case.

Furthermore, if the deceased had indeed disclosed severe ill-treatment on that very night, it would have been natural for the mother either to The State Of Maharashtra vs Madhukar Nana Ghadge And Ors.

4 remove her daughter from the matrimonial home or at least to confront the in-laws.
The admitted conduct of PW-3 in merely advising her daughter not to worry and thereafter leaving the house casts serious doubt upon the veracity of her version.

14. The other relatives examined by the prosecution, namely PW-5, PW-6, PW-7 and PW-8, have also made only vague and omnibus allegations unsupported by specific instances or corroborated by independent evidence.
Their testimonies suffer from exaggerations and contradictions and, in several respects, are inconsistent with the evidence of the deceased's parents.
Consequently, their evidence does not inspire confidence and cannot safely be relied upon to establish cruelty or harassment.
15. Considerable reliance has been placed by the prosecution on the dying declarations allegedly made by the deceased.

A careful scrutiny of the record, however, reveals that the first dying d e c l a r a t i o n d a t e d 1 0 D e c e m b e r 2 0 0 4 ( E x h . 3 8 ) , a s w e l l a s __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx the contemporaneous statement recorded by the police on the same day, do not attribute any blame to the accused.
In those statements, the deceased merely stated that she had poured kerosene upon herself and set herself on fire.
No allegation of harassment or instigation by any of the accused was made therein.
16. A subsequent dying declaration came to be recorded on 14 December 2004 at the instance of the deceased's mother, who alleged that the earlier statement had been made under pressure.
The reliability of this subsequent declaration appears doubtful.
The evidence of the officer who recorded the statement reveals that there was no medical endorsement certifying that the deceased was in a fit mental and physical condition to make such a statement.
The witness admitted that she had not verified with the attending doctor regarding the patient's fitness.
The absence of such certification assumes considerable importance in view of the well-settled principles governing the evidentiary value of dying declarations.
Since a dying declaration is neither recorded on oath nor subjected to cross-examination, it must be scrutinised with great caution.

One of the essential safeguards is the satisfaction of the recording authority that the declarant was in a fit state of mind to make the s t a t e m e n t . I n t h e p r e s e n t c a s e , t h i s f u n d a m e n t a l __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx requirement has not been fulfilled, thereby rendering the subsequent dying declaration inherently doubtful.
17.
Apart from this, the circumstances in which the subsequent declaration was recorded further weaken its evidentiary value.
The witness admitted that several persons, including police personnel and relatives, were present in the vicinity of the patient when the statement was recorded.
This raises the possibility of tutoring or influence, particularly when the earlier statements made by the deceased were entirely exculpatory.
Moreover, the dying declaration recorded by PSI Nikumbh (Exh.43) contains elaborate and minute details concerning events from the time of the marriage.

Considering that the deceased had sustained approximately 87 per cent burn injuries and was in severe pain, it appears highly improbable that she would have been capable of narrating such a detailed and lengthy account.

sentences.text: In any event, even a reading of Exhibit 43 does not disclose any specific act of cruelty or instigation attributable to the accused which could have driven the deceased to commit suicide.

At the highest, it indicates that a quarrel had taken place and that the deceased, in a moment of anger,
s e t h e r s e l f o n f i r e . O n t h e c o n t r a r y , t h e c o n d u c t o f t h e a c c u s e d , a s __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx
reflected
even in the statement of the deceased
, indicates that they attempted to extinguish the fire, took her to the hospital for treatment and informed her parents.
Such conduct is inconsistent with the hypothesis that the accused had instigated or aided the commission of suicide.

19. In order to sustain a conviction under Section 306 of the IPC, the prosecution must establish a clear and proximate act of instigation, aid or intentional conduct on the part of the accused which compelled the deceased to commit suicide.
Mere quarrels or trivial disputes within the matrimonial home do not constitute abetment unless they are of such intensity as to drive the victim to take the extreme step.
Likewise, to attract Section 498-A of the IPC, the prosecution must prove wilful conduct of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury.
The evidence on record falls far short of satisfying this statutory requirement.

20. When the evidence is considered in its entirety, it becomes evident that the prosecution has failed to establish any unlawful demand for dowry or to demonstrate that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty or harassment of such gravity as would drive her to commit suicide.

On the contrary, the evidence indicates that the deceased had been suffering from a __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 Chitra Sonawane. 3-apeal-868-2006.docx psychiatric disorder for several years and was undergoing treatment.
In such circumstances, the possibility that the deceased took the extreme step owing to her mental condition cannot be ruled out.
21. In criminal jurisprudence, the burden rests squarely upon the prosecution to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Where the evidence gives rise to serious doubt and alternative explanations consistent with innocence emerge from the record, the benefit of such doubt must necessarily accrue to the accused.
The learned trial Court, upon a careful appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence, has assigned cogent reasons for extending the benefit of doubt to the accused.
22. In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court finds no compelling or substantial reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order of acquittal passed by the learned trial Court.
The appeal therefore fails and stands dismissed.
[R.N. Laddha, J.] __________________________________________________ 5 March 2026 The State Of Maharashtra vs Madhukar Nana Ghadge And Ors.
